title: Theme Park
goal: Your kid designs a whole theme park or adventure course: the theme, the star rides, the map, the prices and the signs. They build it as a tabletop model, a drawn park or a life-size course in the yard, test it on a real visitor, fix one thing, and hold a grand opening.
need: Cardboard, boxes, paper towel rolls, tape, scissors and string
Paper and markers for the map, signs and tickets
Small toys or figurines as visitors
Outdoor option: chalk, pool noodles, cones, jump ropes, buckets

lesson.text: Where you put things decides how people move. A good park map pulls visitors through the whole park instead of jamming them at the gate.
lesson.before: The roller coaster, the snack stand and the bathrooms are all right by the gate.

model.line: Everyone stops at the gate at once. Instant traffic jam.
Put it at the far end of the park, so people walk past everything else to get there.
Put the snack stand between two thrill rides, where people get hungry.
The map decides where people go, so plan it on purpose.

lesson.modelNote: That's the question behind every step: what does a visitor do here, and where do they go next?

howTo.intro: You don't need teaching experience. You're the visitor, not the designer. Let them pick the theme and build it their way. When they're ready, walk through it as a real guest: your honest confusion or delight is the best feedback they'll get.

plan.what: Pick the theme and rides, and draw the map (Steps 1 and 2).
Build the park and add the details and prices (Steps 3 and 4).
Test it, fix one thing, then open the gates (Step 5).

troubleshoot.q: They want every idea they've ever had
troubleshoot.a: Start with 3 to 5 star attractions. The rest go on a 'coming soon' sign for Season 2.

troubleshoot.q: They spend hours on one ride
troubleshoot.a: That's fine. Some kids perfect one ride, others make five in twenty minutes. The goal is a park someone can tour.

skills.name: Spatial thinking
skills.text: how people move through a space

skills.name: Business sense
skills.text: what visitors want, and what it costs

steps.title: Pick the theme and the star rides
steps.why: One theme, and a few rides worth the trip.
steps.kid: Your kid picks one theme, like a jungle adventure, a space station or a pirate cove, and names 3 to 5 star attractions. They use the Attraction mix card in the Park Designer's Toolkit at the end of the guide to get something thrilling, something calm and something hands-on.
steps.you: Help them commit to one theme instead of cramming in everything. Ask what kind of park they would want to visit.
ask: What's the one ride people would travel far to try?
What do you want visitors talking about on the way home?
steps.tip: Name everything. 'The Jungle Drop' sells better than 'the drop ride,' and naming makes the theme stick.

levels.explore: Pick a theme and draw 3 rides.
levels.develop: Pick a theme and name 4 or 5 rides of at least 3 different kinds.
levels.extend: Plan themed zones, with a star ride and a snack stand in each.

steps.title: Draw the map and plan the flow
steps.why: The map decides where people go.
steps.kid: Your kid draws the park from above on a big sheet: the entrance, the zones, the paths, the food and the bathrooms. Then they walk a finger through it as a pretend visitor and fix where it gets crowded or where nobody would go.
steps.you: Ask about flow: 'I just walked in the gate. Where do I go first?' Let them find the problems with the finger walk.
ask: If 100 people walked in at once, where would the traffic jam be?
What do visitors see first when they come through the gate?
steps.tip: Real parks put a big attraction at the far end so people walk past everything else on the way. Try it.

levels.explore: Draw a map with the entrance, the rides and paths.
levels.develop: Draw a map with zones, food, bathrooms and paths, then do the finger walk.
levels.extend: Use the Map checklist card, and add a one-way route that passes every ride.

steps.title: Build the park
steps.why: The map becomes something you can walk through.
steps.kid: Your kid builds the park their way: a tabletop model (boxes for buildings, tubes for towers, string for zip lines, toys as riders), a drawn park with a blueprint of each ride, or a life-size course in the yard with chalk paths, pool noodle tunnels and cone obstacles.
steps.you: Help with tricky construction, and remind them that working matters more than pretty.
ask: What's the hardest part to build, and how could you simplify it?
Does the build match your map, or did you change things?
steps.tip: For a life-size course, time each visitor and post the results. Kids will run it again and again.

levels.explore: Build 3 attractions any way you like.
levels.develop: Build every star attraction, laid out like the map.
levels.extend: Build it with a working moving part, like a zip line, a ramp or a spinner.

steps.title: Add the details and the prices
steps.why: Signs, tickets and a menu turn rides into a place.
steps.kid: Your kid adds an entrance sign, tickets or wristbands and a menu for at least one food stand, with prices. Then they work out what a family of four would spend in a day. Extras if they want: a gift shop, a mascot or a safety rules poster.
steps.you: Nudge the business side: 'What does a hot dog cost at your park?' Let the maths happen without pointing it out.
ask: What would a family of four spend for a whole day?
What souvenir would people buy to remember it?
steps.tip: Family of 4: tickets 4 × $12 = $48, lunch 4 × $6 = $24, one souvenir $5. That's $77. Would they pay it?

levels.explore: Make a sign, tickets and a menu with prices.
levels.develop: Price everything and work out a family's day total.
levels.extend: Work out wait times: 40 people in line, 8 riders per trip, 2 minutes a trip = 10 minutes.

steps.title: Test it, fix one thing, open the gates
steps.why: A real visitor shows what the plan missed.
steps.kid: Your kid gives someone a full tour: the entrance, a ticket, the paths, every ride. They watch what confuses the visitor, then fix the one thing that would help most. Then the grand opening: a ribbon, the park's name announced, tickets taken, tours given, food served.
steps.you: Be an honest visitor first. Don't fake excitement for parts that don't work yet. On opening day, bring the energy of someone who waited in line all morning.
ask: What part of the tour surprised you?
If you built a second park, what would you change?
steps.tip: Fix one thing, not everything. Pick the change that makes the biggest difference for a visitor.

levels.explore: Give one tour, fix one thing, and open the park.
levels.develop: Run 2 tours, fix the biggest problem, and hold an opening with roles for helpers.
levels.extend: Collect visitor feedback in a guest book, and film a 'welcome to the park' commercial.

after.label: Park rules
lines: One theme, and everything fits it.
The big ride goes at the far end.
Food near the thrills, benches near the food.
After every tour, fix one thing.

conclusion.headline: The park is open.
conclusion.text: Your kid started with a vision, fit it into a real space, built it from whatever was around, priced it, tested it on a real visitor and ran opening day. That's how designers, architects and business owners work: plan, build, test, fix, open.
conclusion.celebrate: Tell them what impressed you: a smart spot on the map, a ride name that made you laugh, or how they ran opening day.
extensions: Design a Season 2 expansion with a new zone
Build a water park, zoo or museum next door
Make a park brochure or a poster
Turn the yard course into a timed challenge and beat your record

signs: They notice how real parks, stores and museums move people around
They work out what a day out would cost
They ask a visitor what confused them, and fix it
makeItReal: Next time you visit a park, zoo or museum, ask them to find where the big attraction is and why it's there. Real designers made the same choices they did.
levelsLine: Every step has three levels: Explore, Develop, Extend. Pick the one that fits your kid today, and change it anytime. Siblings can do the same step at different levels, side by side.
